issues.title: [upstream] Failing test case `TestExportOpInfoCPU.test_fake_export_nn_functional_max_unpool2d_grad_target_device_xpu:0_cpu_float32`
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

On a CPU-only build, propagating fake tensors whose device is `xpu:0` through
`max_unpool2d` fails with:

```
RuntimeError: PyTorch is not linked with support for xpu devices
```

Repro (needs a build with neither XPU nor CUDA linked; no `torch.export`
required, plain fake propagation is enough):

```python
import torch
from torch._subclasses.fake_tensor import FakeTensorMode

x, idx = torch.nn.functional.max_pool2d(torch.randn(1, 2, 3, 6), 3, return_indices=True)
x = x.contiguous(memory_format=torch.channels_last)
idx = idx.contiguous(memory_format=torch.channels_last)

with FakeTensorMode(allow_non_fake_inputs=True):
    torch.nn.functional.max_unpool2d(x.to("xpu:0"), idx.to("xpu:0"), 3, output_size=(1, 2, 3, 6))
```

In CI it shows up as:

```
PYTORCH_OPINFO_SAMPLE_INPUT_INDEX=8 python test/export/test_export_opinfo.py \
    TestExportOpInfoCPU.test_fake_export_nn_functional_max_unpool2d_grad_target_device_xpu:0_cpu_float32
```

## Root cause

`_max_unpoolnd` restrides its output to match the input's memory format, for
`cpu` and `xpu` only, because those are the backends whose native kernels
preserve memory format (`torch/_decomp/decompositions.py`, `_restride`):

```python
def _restride(t: TensorLike) -> TensorLike:
    if dim == 2 and self.device.type in ("cpu", "xpu"):
        return t.contiguous(memory_format=utils.suggest_memory_format(self))
    return t
```

`Tensor.contiguous` is not guard-free. Its generated Python binding wraps the
call in a device guard on the tensor's own device
(`torch/csrc/autograd/generated/python_variable_methods.cpp`):

```cpp
static Tensor dispatch_contiguous(const Tensor & self, at::MemoryFormat memory_format) {
  pybind11::gil_scoped_release no_gil;
  OptionalDeviceGuard device_guard(device_of(self));
  return self.contiguous(memory_format);
}
```

A `FakeTensor` reports its *fake* device, so `device_of(self)` is `xpu:0` and
constructing the guard calls `getDeviceGuardImpl(DeviceType::XPU)`, which throws
on a build with no XPU support linked in.

Two things mask this:

- `THPVariable_contiguous` early-returns before `dispatch_contiguous` when the
  tensor is already contiguous in the requested format, so only samples with a
  non-contiguous (channels-last) input construct the guard. Index 8 is the first
  such OpInfo sample.
- The `cuda` target never enters `_restride` at all, so the pre-existing
  `cuda:0` parametrization of this test has always passed.

There is also an asymmetry worth deciding on here: `FakeTensorMode` calls
`torch._C._ensureCUDADeviceGuardSet()` when `avoid_device_init` is set, but
`c10::impl::ensureCUDADeviceGuardSet()` only installs a `FakeGuardImpl<CUDA>`
when the CUDA guard is already registered and reports 0 devices. It is a no-op
on a CPU-only build, and there is no XPU equivalent.

## Possible fixes

- Make the decomposition guard-free. `torch.ops.aten.contiguous.default(t,
  memory_format=...)`, `t.clone(memory_format=...)` and `aten.clone` all work on
  a fake tensor whose device type is not linked into the build; only the
  `Tensor.contiguous` Python binding does not.
- Or, more generally, register a fake device guard for the device types a
  `FakeTensorMode` is targeting, so any guard-taking binding is safe under fake
  propagation rather than fixing decompositions one at a time.


### Versions

CPU-only build without XPU nor CUDA available.

issues.title: [Bug Skip]: test_ops_xpu.py python_ref ihfft2/ihfftn float16 reference farther than torch result
issues.body:
## Description

Three `test_ops_xpu.py` python-reference cases for `fft.ihfft2`/`fft.ihfftn` fail on XPU with `float16` because the `_refs` reference result is farther from the precise (double-precision) computation than the eager torch result.

This is an accuracy gap (not the empty-batch oneMKL config error tracked in #4980, and not `hfft2` in #3796). The `float16` variants of these specific tests were excluded from the #4980 child-issue series.

## Affected Test Cases

```
test_ops_xpu.py::TestCommonXPU::test_python_ref__refs_fft_ihfft2_xpu_float16
test_ops_xpu.py::TestCommonXPU::test_python_ref__refs_fft_ihfftn_xpu_float16
test_ops_xpu.py::TestCommonXPU::test_python_ref_torch_fallback__refs_fft_ihfftn_xpu_float16
```

## Error Message

```
AssertionError: tensor(False, device='xpu:0') is not true : Reference result was farther (0.0648.../0.0541...) from the precise computation than the torch result was (0.0549.../0.0531...)!

Caused by reference input at index 0:
SampleInput(input=Tensor[size=(2, 8, 16), device="xpu:0", dtype=torch.float16], args=(), kwargs={'s': (4,8), 'dim': (1,2), 'norm': 'ortho'})
```

## Repro

```
PYTORCH_OPINFO_SAMPLE_INPUT_INDEX=0 PYTORCH_TEST_WITH_SLOW=1 \
  python test/test_ops.py TestCommonXPU::test_python_ref__refs_fft_ihfft2_xpu_float16
```

## Related

- #4980 (empty-batch oneMKL FFT error, different root cause)
- #3796 (same symptom class for hfft2, CLOSED/skipped)

---

nodes.bodyText:
Root cause.
oneMKL has no float16 DFT, so torch-xpu-ops emulates one: it upcasts to float32, does the transform and the normalization there, and rounds to complex32 once at the end. But pytorch#171231 added "xpu" to maybe_support_half, which tells the reference implementation that XPU supports half natively. So the ref stays in float16 and rounds at every prim boundary, while eager secretly computed in float32. test_python_ref then asserts ref_error <= eager_error with no tolerance at all, and the ref loses: ihfftn is 1.18x worse, ihfft2 1.02x. Only 1 of 10 samples is affected. The kernel is not broken, it is more accurate than true float16 would be. No user is affected either, since inductor promotes fp16 FFT to float32 (pytorch#180766) and compiled output is bit-identical to eager.
Proposed fix.
There is nothing to fix in the XPU kernel, so this is about how the test expresses a legitimate backend difference. The right thing to do now is declare the skip properly in the OpInfo, which is small, safe and matches what upstream already does for CUDA. The real problem, though, is the test framework itself: a tolerance-free comparison cannot express "this backend computes in higher precision". That is worth fixing eventually, but it is far too broad to attach to this issue.
A. DecorateInfo fix, for now. Add 5 xpu-scoped, float16-only DecorateInfo skips beside the existing cuda ones in torch/testing/_internal/opinfo/definitions/fft.py, carrying the oneMKL reason and a link here. Pure addition, no change to CUDA, no rebuild. It adds no coverage, but it makes XPU's reason explicit instead of inherited from CUDA, and it keeps upstream CI green as @skipXPU is progressively removed from test_ops.py.
B. Test refactor, for the future. Add a tolerance to the ref_error <= eager_error assertion, which pytorch has wanted since May 2022 (pytorch#78026, "TODO: consider adding some tolerance to this comparison"). It treats the cause and would let CUDA, ROCm and XPU all delete skips. But that single assertion guards every test_python_ref case on every backend and dtype, and too loose a tolerance hides the real reference bugs it exists to catch, so it needs primTorch owners and extensive testing across all backends before anything changes.

Sub-item
Verdict

Root Cause
Sub-item 1 — test_effn_attn_uniform_zero_bias

Target repo: pytorch (analyzed at 31527a43)
Domains: inductor, xpu-kernel

The test's third phase traces F.scaled_dot_product_attention(..., attn_mask=padding_mask) under sdpa_kernel(SDPBackend.EFFICIENT_ATTENTION) and asserts that exactly one aten._scaled_dot_product_efficient_attention node reaches the joint graph (test_cuda_repro.py:298, driven from :328). On XPU no such node is ever created: select_sdp_backend_xpu returns the math backend from its efficient_attention case (aten/src/ATen/native/mkldnn/xpu/Attention.cpp:224-231, with a TORCH_WARN_ONCE stating the mem-efficient backend is unsupported on XPU), so the call traces to the math decomposition and len(biases) is 0. The test's first two phases pass because they invoke aten._scaled_dot_product_efficient_attention.default directly and bypass backend selection. PLATFORM_SUPPORTS_MEM_EFF_ATTENTION is nonetheless true on XPU (torch/testing/_internal/common_cuda.py:207-222), so the existing gate does not exclude the test.

Fix strategy: skip the test on XPU with a tracking issue. Making _fused_sdp_choice_xpu actually select efficient_attention is a capability and performance change (the XPU efficient backward re-runs the whole math forward under autograd), which belongs to the XPU SDPA owners.

Sub-item 2 — test_effn_attn_uniform_zero_bias_backward

Target repo: torch-xpu-ops (analyzed at d6fa1aaa, the commit pinned by third_party/xpu.txt at pytorch 31527a43)
Domains: xpu-kernel, inductor

Compiled code asserts the strides that the meta (fake) kernel promised, and XPU's backward does not deliver them. meta__scaled_dot_product_efficient_backward allocates grad_q/k/v with torch.empty_permuted((B, H, S, D), (0, 2, 1, 3)) (torch/_meta_registrations.py:6835-6852), i.e. BHSD sizes over BSHD-contiguous memory — strides (H*S*D, D, H*D, 1), which for [2, 4, 128, 64] is (32768, 64, 256, 1). XPU's _scaled_dot_product_efficient_attention_backward_xpu computes gradients by re-running the math forward under autograd and returns them untouched (src/ATen/native/transformers/Attention.cpp:635-652), so they come back plain contiguous — (32768, 8192, 64, 1). Inductor's assert_size_stride on the backward outputs then fails with exactly the expected (..., 64, 256, 1) / got (..., 8192, 64, 1) mismatch in the CI log.
That the contract is a real layout requirement, not a meta-kernel quirk, is visible on the CUDA side: _efficient_attention_backward returns grad_q.transpose(1, 2) etc. off BSHD-allocated buffers (aten/src/ATen/native/transformers/cuda/attention_backward.cu:1131-1132) and its chunked path allocates with the same at::empty_permuted(..., {0, 2, 1, 3}) (:1144-1147). The XPU forward already normalizes its own output this exact way — attention.permute({0,2,1,3}).contiguous().permute({0,2,1,3}) (src/ATen/native/transformers/Attention.cpp:468-469) — the backward simply never got the same treatment.

Fix strategy: apply the same permute/contiguous/permute normalization to grad_q, grad_k and grad_v before returning them from _scaled_dot_product_efficient_attention_backward_xpu. grad_bias is left alone: the meta pads its last dimension up to a multiple of 16 before slicing, and the bias in this test is [2, 4, 128, 128] whose last dim is already aligned, so autograd's contiguous result matches. (An unaligned bias width would be a separate, currently untested gap.)

Automated by fix-root-cause.



Implement — sub-item 1

Target repo: pytorch @ 31527a43
Changed: test/inductor/test_cuda_repro.py — @skipIfXpu(msg=...) on CudaReproTests.test_effn_attn_uniform_zero_bias, message citing the tracking issue.
Skip added: yes — tracking issue #5329 records the real capability gap (XPU SDPA never selects the efficient-attention backend).

         not PLATFORM_SUPPORTS_MEM_EFF_ATTENTION,

Analyzed at torch-xpu-ops@1a18a331, pytorch origin/main@7280527.
scatter_fill_kernel calls ScatterFillBaseKernel<>()(..., tensor_assign)
(src/ATen/native/xpu/sycl/ScatterGatherKernels.cpp:755). ScatterFillBaseKernel
had only two operator() overloads: a generic template <typename func_t> one and

float8 scalar scatter", pytorch/pytorch#197199) added
dtypesIfCUDA=all_types_complex_float8_and(torch.bool, torch.half, torch.bfloat16)
to OpInfo('scatter'). OpInfo.supported_dtypes() returns
dtypesIf.get(device_type, dtypes) and XPU inherits dtypesIfCUDA when
dtypesIfXPU is unset, so the four float8 parametrizations of
test_overrides.py::test_redispatch started running on XPU and hitting sample
index 8, the scatter.value scalar-fill sample.
The same upstream commit fixed CUDA by adding a dedicated TensorAssign overload
to _cuda_scatter_fill_base_kernel that dispatches via AT_DISPATCH_V2 with
AT_EXPAND(AT_FLOAT8_TYPES) (aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/ScatterGatherKernel.cu:513-554).

ScatterGatherBaseKernel (ScatterGatherKernels.cpp:404, which is where fp8
support for the tensor-source scatter/gather path comes from); only the

Root Cause
Analyzed at pytorch origin/main@8224fee7.
test/inductor/test_compile_subprocess.py re-runs the whole CommonTemplate suite with fx_compile_mode = SUBPROCESS, so every graph has to be serialized by GraphPickler (torch/fx/_graph_pickler.py:216). When dill is importable it replaces the stdlib pickler there (torch/fx/_graph_pickler.py:13-18). dill decides whether a function can be stored by reference with _locate_function, which resolves a dotted module name by importing the parent package and doing getattr(parent, last_component). For torch._higher_order_ops.invoke_subgraph that getattr does not return the submodule: torch/_higher_order_ops/__init__.py binds the name invoke_subgraph to the InvokeSubgraphHOP instance, shadowing the module of the same name. Every function and class defined in torch/_higher_order_ops/invoke_subgraph.py therefore looks unresolvable to dill, which falls back to pickling them by value; walking their __globals__ eventually reaches a _thread._local and pickling dies. Confirmed directly: dill._dill._locate_function returns False for invoke_subgraph.get_backward_nested_region_config but True for torch._higher_order_ops.utils.saved_values, and dill emits PicklingWarning: Cannot locate reference to <class 'torch._higher_order_ops.invoke_subgraph.NestedCompileRegionOptions'> on the way down.
This test is the only one in CommonTemplate that puts such objects into the graph: it is the only case calling get_invoke_subgraph_compile_options() (torch/_higher_order_ops/invoke_subgraph.py:1480-1516), which hangs two functools.partial compiler callables off NestedCompileRegionOptions. Nothing about the path is device dependent, and the file already declares the test as expected-to-fail-and-skip on the other two devices -- "test_regional_fallback_by_default_invoke_subgraph": TestFailure(("cpu", "cuda"), is_skip=True) with a comment naming this exact dill by-value fallback (test/inductor/test_compile_subprocess.py:76-87, added by pytorch/pytorch#194704). xpu was simply left out of that tuple, so XPU CI is the only configuration still running a test that is known-broken everywhere, which is what got it auto-disabled by pytorch/pytorch#195876.
The genuine fix is not in pytorch source: newer dill honours byref for functions as well as classes, and the test passes unmodified under dill==0.4.1 (verified in this container). Making it pass under the CI-pinned dill==0.3.7 would require either bumping dill in .ci/docker/requirements-ci.txt -- a repo-wide dependency change that rebuilds every CI image and also changes the other four is_skip entries in this same dict -- or teaching GraphPickler to force by-reference function saving, which changes fx-graph serialization for every backend. Both are maintainer decisions, so this run aligns the XPU expectation with cpu/cuda instead and records the dill finding for the follow-up.

Target repository: pytorch/pytorch (test infrastructure, test/dynamo/test_fx_graph_runnable.py)
Analyzed sha: 8ffdc987663f953bca8934ff07b1df3f8ccebbd7 (origin/main)

FxGraphRunnableTest._exec_and_verify_payload writes the captured fx_graph_runnable payload to a temp file and runs it in a fresh Python process with a hard-coded timeout=45. The base torch._inductor.test_case.TestCase wraps every test in fresh_cache(), so the payload inherits a brand-new TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR / TRITON_CACHE_DIR and can never hit a warm cache. That 45s budget therefore has to cover, from cold, in a fresh interpreter: import torch, XPU runtime init, the inductor compile of the graph, and a JIT compile of every user-defined Triton kernel the graph references.
test_multi_kernel_nesting_and_global_constexpr is one of the two heaviest tests in the file by that measure -- its graph carries four separate user-defined Triton kernels. Measured on this runner: ~3s for import torch plus XPU init, and 14-20s total for the payload. The XPU CI machine (PVC, linux.idc.xpu) is roughly 2.5x slower through the Triton compile path, which puts it over 45s -- exactly what the job log shows, three reruns in a row.
This is a known, recurring shape rather than a new bug. pytorch/pytorch#170292 ("Enlarge dynamo UT timeout for XPU due to low CPU freq of XPU CI machine") already raised this same constant from 30s to 45s to close pytorch/pytorch#169924 and pytorch/pytorch#163595, and 14 DISABLED ... FxGraphRunnableTest issues have been filed for XPU on this file. The 1.5x bump was simply not enough for the two Triton-kernel-heavy tests, which are precisely the two still open: pytorch/pytorch#196392 and pytorch/pytorch#196899.
Fix strategy: give the payload subprocess a larger budget on XPU only, so the bound stays tight for CUDA/CPU where 45s is already generous. No product code is involved -- the failure is purely the harness's wall-clock budget.

is_capture_context() returns false when the block is freed on the joined side stream, so insert_events runs mid-capture. Refuted: the side queue is genuinely in queue_state::recording, and the block is deferred as intended (see above).
empty_cache() frees a side-stream allocation that XPU's narrower capture filter left in the default pool while a finalized graph still references it. XPU's capture_begin filter requires queue == &capture_stream_.queue(), unlike CUDA's cudaStreamGetCaptureInfo-based filter which matches any stream in the same capture, so allocations made on a joined side stream do land in the default pool. But holding the side-stream tensor alive across empty_cache() versus dropping it made no difference -- both completed cleanly. Not confirmed as a cause. (Worth a maintainer's eye as a latent divergence from CUDA, but it is not what this test is failing on.)

Root Cause
Analyzed at pytorch origin/main@6a895d1264e.
torch/xpu/_utils.py:39 forwards an unspecified device to the generic
torch._utils._get_device_index, which resolves device=None through
_get_current_device_index -> _get_device_attr -> _get_available_device_type
(torch/_utils.py:820-858). That generic resolver returns "cuda" whenever
torch.cuda.is_available() is true, so the XPU helper ends up calling
torch.cuda.current_device(). The test patches torch.cuda.is_available to
True (to let check_versions accept a cuda entry on a host without a cuda
device), so on an XPU runner torch.xpu.get_device_name() raises
AssertionError: Torch not compiled with CUDA enabled from
torch/cuda/__init__.py:_lazy_init.
That exception is swallowed by the except Exception: pass in
SystemInfo.current (torch/_dynamo/package.py:790-796), which therefore
records toolkit_version=None, gpu_name=None instead of the XPU stamp. The
saved entry carries the real torch.version.xpu, so
SystemInfo.check_compatibility fails with
RuntimeError: Compile package was created with a different toolkit version.
Nothing cuda-specific is involved in the package logic itself -- the test is new
(added by pytorch/pytorch#196814, c611a4b556e), and it is the first caller to
put torch.cuda.is_available() == True in front of an XPU device query.
torch/mtia/_utils.py:23-25 already avoids this by short-circuiting
device is None and optional to its own runtime's current device instead of the
generic resolver. The fix applies that same shape to torch/xpu/_utils.py, which
also removes the latent bug for real dual-runtime builds (a cuda-enabled build
would hand a cuda device index to every torch.xpu.*(device=None) call).

Tricubic sampling (mode='bicubic' with a 5D input) has an implementation upstream for CPU (aten/src/ATen/native/GridSampler.cpp) and CUDA (aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/GridSampler.cu, which has dedicated grid_sampler_3d_bicubic_kernel / grid_sampler_3d_bicubic_backward_kernel). The refusal comes from a legacy 3-argument overload in ATen/native/GridSamplerUtils.h, whose only job is to raise TORCH_CHECK_NOT_IMPLEMENTED for bicubic and which carries the comment "TODO: drop this overload once torch-xpu-ops stops calling it. torch-xpu-ops passes the mode; in-tree backends call the overload above and refuse bicubic themselves." torch-xpu-ops was the last caller: src/ATen/native/xpu/sycl/GridSampler.cpp used it in both grid_sampler_3d_kernel and grid_sampler_3d_backward_kernel, so every 5D bicubic call on XPU failed at the check before any kernel ran.
The OpInfo sample_inputs_grid_sample generates bicubic samples for both dim=2 and dim=3, which is how sample index 30 lands on the unimplemented 5D case; the four failing tests differ only in dtype.

Implement
Ported the CUDA tricubic kernels to SYCL instead of keeping the refusal, per the domain rule that a missing XPU kernel is implemented in line with CUDA rather than skipped.

src/ATen/native/xpu/sycl/GridSampler.h -- four device helpers the taps need: grid_sampler_unnormalize_sized, grid_sampler_unnormalize_set_grad_sized, compute_coordinates_sized, and resolve_cubic_taps (the device twin of the same-named helper in upstream ATen/native/GridSampler.cpp). These take the extent in index_t and skip the safe_downgrade_to_int_range step, so a tap past INT_MAX keeps its voxel instead of being poisoned.
src/ATen/native/xpu/sycl/GridSampler.cpp -- grid_sampler_3d_bicubic_kernel_func and grid_sampler_3d_bicubic_backward_kernel_func plus their submit templates, and the two dispatch sites switched to the 2-argument check_grid_sampler_3d(input, grid) with the mode now selecting the bicubic kernel.

Bicubic gets kernels of its own rather than a third branch inside the existing grid_sampler_3d_kernel_func, matching CUDA: a tricubic sample reads 64 taps against a trilinear sample's 8, and getKernelMaxWorkGroupSize is resolved per kernel, so folding them together would cost the trilinear path occupancy on every call.
Where CUDA uses fastAtomicAdd, the SYCL backward uses the plain atomicAdd from sycl/Atomics.h -- torch-xpu-ops has no fastAtomicAdd, and the taps resolve_cubic_taps returns are already resolved to in-bounds indices, so no bounds guard is needed on the add.

Root Cause
Analyzed at pytorch origin/main@2e9b4aff8d.
test/inductor/test_flex_decoding.py turns on oneDNN TF32 process-wide at import time (torch._C._set_onednn_allow_tf32(True), test/inductor/test_flex_decoding.py:111), and test_pointwise_query_producer is decorated @with_tf32_off. But tf32_off() in torch/testing/_internal/common_cuda.py:449 only clears the CUDA and cuDNN knobs: it sets torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False and enters torch.backends.cudnn.flags(allow_tf32=False), and its _save_matmul_precision/_restore_matmul_precision pair carries only the legacy Float32MatmulPrecision enum plus the two fp32_precision values. The oneDNN flag is a separate Context member, allow_tf32_onednn (aten/src/ATen/Context.h:538), which Context::setFloat32MatmulPrecision (aten/src/ATen/Context.cpp:485) never writes, so nothing in tf32_off reaches it.
The consequence is a split precision inside one assertion. The eager reference f(x, k, v) runs its matmuls through oneDNN, which selects dnnl::fpmath_mode::tf32 whenever allowTF32OneDNN() is true (aten/src/ATen/native/mkldnn/xpu/detail/Matmul.cpp:201), while the compiled branch goes through Inductor's flex lowering, where set_float32_precision (torch/_inductor/kernel/flex/flex_attention.py:131) reads torch.backends.cuda.matmul.fp32_precision -- which tf32_off did clear -- and emits FLOAT32_PRECISION='ieee' into the Triton template. So assertEqual compares a TF32 eager result against an IEEE compiled result at default fp32 tolerances (atol=1e-5, rtol=1.3e-6). On PVC that gap is ~1e-3; on BMG both paths are IEEE regardless of the flag, which is why the test is green here.
Emulating PVC by truncating the eager inputs' mantissas to 10 bits reproduces the CI regime exactly: IEEE-vs-IEEE gives 0/1024 mismatched at max_abs=2.4e-7, while TF32-eager-vs-IEEE-compiled gives 1009/1024 at max_abs=2.7e-3 and max_rel=0.215 -- the same shape as the reported 968/1024, 1.14e-3, 0.198. The fix is in tf32_off(): it must also disable the oneDNN flag on XPU, the way test/inductor/test_flex_attention.py:147-171 already maps a "highest" request to torch._C._set_onednn_allow_tf32(False). torch.backends.mkldnn is a bracketed-mutation PropModule, so the flag has to be driven through torch.backends.mkldnn.flags(...) as a context manager rather than by assignment -- the same shape as the existing cudnn.flags handling two lines above.

Root Cause
Analyzed at pytorch origin/main@958e9824.
test_combo_kernel_per_config_subkernel_r0_r1 (test/inductor/test_combo_kernels.py:825-839) compares an eager a.sum(dim=(1, 2)) against the torch.compile result with a bare self.assertEqual(out_eager, out_compiled) at test/inductor/test_combo_kernels.py:837, i.e. with torch.testing's default float32 tolerances (atol=1e-5, rtol=1.3e-6). The inputs are torch.randn(32, 16, 64).permute(1, 0, 2), so each of the 16 outputs is a float32 sum of 2048 standard normals. Under the test's triton.prefer_nd_tiling + triton.tile_reductions config the Triton kernel accumulates that sum as a tiled 2D (r0_, r1_) reduction, which is a different summation order from the eager reduction, so the two results differ by float32 rounding noise. That is exactly what CI sees: element 15 has value ~0.82 while the sum of the absolute values feeding it is ~1.6e3, i.e. near-total cancellation, so the rtol=1.3e-6 bound is meaningless there and the atol=1e-5 bound is just barely exceeded (observed 1.1444e-05).
Neither side is wrong. Measured against a float64 reference of the same reduction, the eager result is off by up to 8.9e-06 and the compiled result by up to 1.1e-05; relative to the ~1.6e3 sum of absolute values both are ~6e-09, i.e. ordinary float32 accumulation error for a 2048-element reduction. The test is simply the only reduction test in this file that forgot to pass tolerances: the two sibling tests added by the same PR, test_combo_kernel_per_config_subkernel_per (test/inductor/test_combo_kernels.py:783) and test_combo_kernel_per_config_subkernel_red (test/inductor/test_combo_kernels.py:806), compare their eager/compiled sums with torch.testing.assert_close(..., atol=1e-4, rtol=1e-4).
The test was introduced by pytorch/pytorch#171671 ("[inductor] Add per-sub-kernel block dimensions for combo kernels"), which is also what makes it run twice: ComboKernelTestsPerSubkernelBlocks (test/inductor/test_combo_kernels.py:1954) subclasses ComboKernelTests, so both pytorch/pytorch#198180 and pytorch/pytorch#198181 are the same assertion. The fix is to give that one comparison the same explicit tolerances the sibling reduction tests already use.

What the bug was. pytorch/pytorch#198709 disables test_load_then_compile_survives_baked_in_global_collision on xpu; it fails with AssertionError: Subprocess failure (KeyError: '__builtins__'). GraphRuntimeEnv.forward_callable builds the Dynamo-generated function's __globals__ as a plain dict with no __builtins__ key. On a machine with an accelerator the generated pre-graph bytecode opens with store_user_object_weakrefs(get_current_stream(torch.device('xpu', 0))), and torch._dynamo.utils.get_current_stream is now a pybind function instead of a Python one — so there is no intermediate Python frame. The accelerator's device_lazy_init reaches PyImport_ImportModule("torch.xpu"), and CPython's PyImport_Import reads __builtins__ off the calling frame's globals with PyObject_GetItem, which raises KeyError on a dict that lacks it. Only the load path trips (an in-process compile has already initialized the device), and it is xpu-only because that is the CI configuration which runs test/dynamo/ on a box with an accelerator.
Fix. Seed __builtins__ into that globals dict before the function object is created, first in the literal so a recorded or caller-supplied binding still wins. I chose this over hardening device_lazy_init because PyImport_ImportModule is reached from many places in torch's C++, so making Dynamo's synthesized namespace look like a real module namespace fixes the whole class. Added test_loaded_bytecode_globals_carry_the_live_builtins, which pins the invariant on the namespace so it fails on any machine.

Root Cause
Target repository: pytorch (test infrastructure) - analyzed at 50ca38ec.
test/inductor/test_flex_decoding.py turns oneDNN TF32 on globally for XPU when the
module is imported (torch._C._set_onednn_allow_tf32(True), line 111), and nothing ever
turns it off again.
test_pointwise_query_producer is the only test in that file that compares the compiled
kernel against the eager reference at assertEqual's default fp32 tolerances
(atol=1e-5, rtol=1.3e-6); every other fp32 comparison there uses atol=rtol=2e-1 or a
float64 golden with a fudge factor. It carries @with_tf32_off precisely so that tight
comparison is legitimate - the PR that added it notes the decorator is needed because the
module-level set_float32_matmul_precision("high") otherwise costs ~2e-3.
On XPU that decorator only does half its job:

tf32_off() (torch/testing/_internal/common_cuda.py:449) resets
torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 and the cuDNN flag, and saves/restores
torch.backends.{cuda,mkldnn}.matmul.fp32_precision.
XPU's oneDNN TF32 switch is a separate global - Context::allow_tf32_onednn
(aten/src/ATen/Context.cpp:290), reachable only through
torch.backends.mkldnn.allow_tf32 / torch._C._set_onednn_allow_tf32. It is not part of
the fp32_precision hierarchy, so neither set_float32_matmul_precision nor
tf32_off() touches it.

and a broken ieee would redden many fp32 inductor matmul tests on PVC CI, which are

The CI log for pytorch/pytorch#199140 shows the same defect manifesting as torch.OutOfMemoryError: XPU out of memory. Tried to allocate 130290.75 GiB (job log). Both symptoms come from one uninitialized read: the kernel derives its reduction extent from an out-of-bounds TensorInfo slot, so the value is whatever happened to be on the stack -- a huge number on the PVC CI runner (OOM), a small one here (silently wrong results). The 2-D shapes in the same test match CPU exactly, which isolates the defect to the 1-D case.

Root Cause
Analyzed at torch-xpu-ops@51acfc9f, pytorch origin/main@18a1d563.
The fused XPU weight_norm kernels derive their launch geometry from a collapsed TensorInfo and assume the input always collapses to two dimensions -- the kept dim and the reduction dim. weight_norm_kernel collapses v around dim, then flips to the surviving reduction dim with dim_after_collapse = 1 - dim_after_collapse and reads vinfo.sizes[dim_after_collapse] as the reduction extent (src/ATen/native/xpu/sycl/WeightNormKernels.cpp:379-401). For a 1-D v with dim=0 the collapse leaves dims == 1, so that index is 1 -- one past the end of the populated part of the info. TensorInfo's constructor only writes sizes[0..dims) (src/comm/TensorInfo.h:90-91, :106-116), so the kernel picks up whatever was on the stack: on the PVC CI runner a huge value, which made the carrier allocation ask for 130290.75 GiB and throw torch.OutOfMemoryError; on the BMG box used here a small value, which silently produced garbage norms. weight_norm_backward_kernel had the same read. Upstream CUDA never hits this because it computes the reduction extent arithmetically -- rowSize = prod(v.size(i) for i in ndims-1..1), an empty product of 1 for a 1-D v (aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/WeightNorm.cu:361-363).
The test appeared on 2026-09-29 with the upstream fix for pytorch/pytorch#198676 (an Inductor decomposition bug for 1-D weight_norm). It was the first test to call eager _weight_norm_interface with a 1-D v on XPU, which is why the latent out-of-bounds read only surfaced now, and why both disable issues point at the same eager line rather than at anything Inductor does.
This is already fixed on torch-xpu-ops main. #5598 (merged 2026-10-05) appends a trivial size-1 reduction dim when dim_after_collapse >= vinfo.dims, in both the forward and the backward path, and adds test/regressions/test_weight_norm.py. That commit is not in pytorch's third_party/xpu.txt pin yet -- the pin is still 5934d4f5 (2026-09-25) -- so pytorch CI and the nightly wheels keep hitting the old code. There is no new patch to author here; the remaining work is the pin bump.

Root cause
nextafter stepping the smallest subnormal toward zero must return a zero carrying the sign of the first argument (nextafter(-5e-324, 0.0) == -0.0). SYCL's device std::nextafter returns +0.0 for float/double, so the eager XPU kernel in src/ATen/native/xpu/sycl/StepKernels.cpp:23 disagreed with CPU/CUDA/Inductor on 6 of the 100 non-NaN cases. Inductor's own fp32 (bit-stepping) and fp64 (libdevice.nextafter) paths were already correct — the test compares eager against compiled, so the failure was purely eager-side. Half/BFloat16 were unaffected (they promote to float and round back to a signed zero).
Fix
NextafterFunctor re-applies the sign of a when the result is zero and a is not — the only case where IEEE 754 yields a zero from a non-zero input — gated with if constexpr (std::is_floating_point_v<scalar_t>). Plus a regression test test/regressions/test_nextafter_signed_zero.py.

+// compute_coordinates with the extent in int64_t and the reflection parity
+// taken by fmod: an int fold count is undefined past INT_MAX, and no float
+// converts to an integer here, so a position past INT_MAX keeps its voxel.
+template <typename scalar_t>
+static inline scalar_t compute_coordinates_sized(
+    scalar_t coord,
+    int64_t size,
+    GridSamplerPadding padding_mode,
+    bool align_corners) {
+  if (padding_mode == GridSamplerPadding::Border) {
+    coord = clip_coordinates(coord, size);
+  } else if (padding_mode == GridSamplerPadding::Reflection) {
+    // the bounds reflect_coordinates halves, formed without doubling the extent
+    const scalar_t low =
+        align_corners ? static_cast<scalar_t>(0) : static_cast<scalar_t>(-0.5);
+    const scalar_t span =
+        static_cast<scalar_t>(align_corners ? size - 1 : size);
+    if (span == 0) {
+      coord = 0;
+    } else {
+      const scalar_t in = sycl::fabs(coord - low);
+      const scalar_t extra = sycl::fmod(in, span);
+      const bool odd =
+          sycl::fmod(sycl::floor(in / span), static_cast<scalar_t>(2)) != 0;
+      coord = odd ? span - extra + low : extra + low;
+    }
+    coord = clip_coordinates(coord, size);
+  }
+  return coord;
+}
+
+// The four cubic taps one axis contributes at `coord`: the Keys coefficients
+// of its fractional part, the index each tap reads, and, when `coeffs_grad` is
+// given, the coefficient derivatives. The taps sit around the unclipped index.
+// A tap the padding drops takes a negative index, contributes a zero value and
+// keeps its coefficient, as get_value_bounded does in 4-D.
+template <typename scalar_t, typename index_t>
+static inline void resolve_cubic_taps(
+    scalar_t coord,
+    index_t size,
+    GridSamplerPadding padding_mode,
+    bool align_corners,
+    scalar_t coeffs[4],
+    scalar_t* coeffs_grad,
+    index_t indices[4]) {
+  const scalar_t base = sycl::floor(coord);
+  get_cubic_upsample_coefficients<scalar_t>(coeffs, coord - base);
+  if (coeffs_grad != nullptr) {
+    get_cubic_coefficients_grad<scalar_t>(coeffs_grad, coord - base);
+  }
+  const scalar_t index_limit =
+      static_cast<scalar_t>(std::numeric_limits<index_t>::max());
+  for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
+    const scalar_t tap = at::native::xpu::compute_coordinates_sized(
+        base - 1 + i, size, padding_mode, align_corners);
+    // a tap that is not finite, or past the index type, fails before the cast
+    const index_t index = (tap >= 0 && tap < index_limit)
+        ? static_cast<index_t>(tap)
+        : static_cast<index_t>(-1);
+    indices[i] = index < size ? index : static_cast<index_t>(-1);
+  }
+}

Analyzed at pytorch origin/main@a49d6be19d.
linalg.tensorinv's OpInfo carries an unittest.expectedFailure for TestCommon
/ test_numpy_ref on device_type="xpu" / torch.float64
(torch/testing/_internal/opinfo/definitions/linalg.py:2650-2657, commented
torch-xpu-ops/issues/4313). test_numpy_ref
(test/test_ops.py:458-473) now compares torch.linalg.tensorinv against
np.linalg.tensorinv successfully on XPU, and unittest converts a pass under
expectedFailure into a hard Unexpected success failure. The op itself is not
broken: over both of the OpInfo's reference inputs -- (2, 2, 3, 12, 1) with
ind=3 (the exact sample quoted in #4313) and
(4, 3, 6, 1, 2) with ind=2 -- the largest relative deviation from NumPy is
1.8e-14, versus the 107.5 reported when the decoration was added.
torch.linalg.inv runs natively on XPU here (no XPUFallback warning with
PYTORCH_DEBUG_XPU_FALLBACK=1), so the correct result comes from the XPU
oneMKL LAPACK path, not from a CPU fallback.
Why it surfaced now: the decoration landed 2026-08-20
(02dbce8ad5, pytorch/pytorch#178849), and the upstream disable was filed
2026-10-08. In between, .ci/docker/common/install_xpu.sh moved the CI
toolchain from Intel oneAPI Deep Learning Essentials 2026.1.2.25 to
2026.1.3.17 on 2026-09-18 (43f512a1c4, pytorch/pytorch#195128), which
carries a new oneMKL. That bump is consistent with the LAPACK inverse numerics
being corrected underneath the still-present xfail; no torch-xpu-ops commit in
that window touches the linalg.inv path
(src/ATen/native/xpu/mkl/BatchLinearAlgebra.cpp last changed 2026-08-12).

entry so test_numpy_ref runs as an ordinary passing test again. The
fix is entirely in pytorch test infrastructure; torch-xpu-ops has no skip or
decoration for this test.

The case is numerics, not an inductor mutation-ordering bug.
foreach_reads_sibling_target builds a = x @ w1, b = x @ w2 on 1024x1024
float32 inputs and checks the compiled _foreach_add_([a, b], [b, a]) against
an eager reference that applies the elements one at a time. The generated code
calls the same aten::mm the reference does:
buf0 = empty_strided_xpu((1024, 1024), (1024, 1), torch.float32)
extern_kernels.mm(x_1, w1_1, out=buf0)
buf1 = empty_strided_xpu((1024, 1024), (1024, 1), torch.float32)
extern_kernels.mm(x_1, w2_1, out=buf1)
triton_poi_fused_0.run(buf0, buf1, buf0, buf1, 1048576, ...)

so a = mm1 + mm2 is an exact float32 add on both sides and the comparison
holds only while both sides accumulate the 1024 products of each mm in the
same order. On the Data Center GPU Max they do not, and the test compares with
assertEqual's float32 tolerance (atol=1e-05, rtol=1.3e-06). The element
that fails is one where the two products cancel -- |a| = 0.41 out of an
accumulation of magnitude ~32 -- so rtol buys nothing there and a normal
reduction-order difference of 1.5e-05 lands outside atol. That is exactly
the reported failure: 1 element of 1048576, greatest absolute difference
1.52587890625e-05 against 1e-05 allowed, on item [0] (a). Item [1]
(b = mm2 + a) carries the same absolute error but larger values, so rtol
covers it.

Fix strategy: draw the inputs of the two mm-based foreach cases from a
small integer range. 1024 products in [-4, 4] sum to at most 4096 and the
foreach adds stay under 2^24, so both matmuls are exact in float32 and the

about mutation ordering, and this keeps its comparison exact rather than
trading it for a tolerance that the next backend reassociation would need
re-tuning. The 1024x1024 shape that exposes the cross-block read is unchanged.
The file already uses integer inputs for the same reason in
test_index_put_as_masked_fill_mask_reads_target_by_extern_kernel and
test_mutable_op_layout_copy_written_back_in_place.

Root Cause
Analyzed at pytorch origin/main@3eeaf1275c.
foreach_reads_sibling_target (test/inductor/test_torchinductor.py:11893) builds
its two values with a 1024x1024x1024 float32 matmul, computes the reference in
eager and the result through compile_fx_inner, and compares them with
assertEqual's float32 tolerances (atol 1e-5, rtol 1.3e-6). Eager's
x @ w1 and inductor's extern_kernels.mm(x, w1, out=buf0) are two separate
aten::mm calls on identical operands, and nothing makes them accumulate in the
same order. On PVC they do not: one or two of the 1048576 elements land about
1.5e-5 apart, which is over atol, at an element that moves from run to run.
The mutation semantics the test exists to check are not involved. The generated
wrapper issues the two extern mms into buf0 / buf1 and then one pointwise
kernel which, per index, does tmp2 = buf0 + buf1; tmp3 = buf1 + tmp2 and stores
them back -- exactly the order the test's add_in_order reference applies, with
no cross-index dependency and so no race. Everything after the matmul is
therefore bit-exact, which was confirmed here: when both matmuls agree, the
compiled and eager outputs are bitwise equal.
So the test's only inexact ingredient is the matmul, and it asks two independent
GEMM invocations to agree to within a float32 atol over a million elements. The
fix is to stop asking: integer-valued inputs keep both matmuls exact, which is
the trick test_index_put_as_masked_fill_mask_reads_target_by_extern_kernel in
the same file already uses ("Integer values keep the mm, and so the mask, exact
in low precision").

Test: inductor/test_torchinductor.py::GPUTests::test_mutate_realized_buffer_in_make_fx_graph_case_foreach_reads_sibling_target_xpu
CI failure (Max 1100 / PVC): Tensor-likes are not close! — 1 of 1048576
elements, greatest abs diff 1.53e-05 (allowed 1e-05), rel diff 5.35e-06
(allowed 1.3e-06).
Root cause. The case compares a = x @ w1, b = x @ w2 (1024x1024 fp32)
after an in-place _foreach_add_, using assertEqual's default float32
tolerance (rtol=1.3e-6, atol=1e-5). Nothing makes inductor's extern mm
and eager's mm round a 1024-long fp32 reduction the same way, and on the
Max 1100 they don't: one element landed about 4 ULPs of the partial sums apart,
on a value of 2.854. Both results are valid fp32 matmuls — no XPU operator is
wrong, the comparison is simply tighter than the arithmetic allows.
Fix. The two cases whose expected values come out of an mm
(foreach_reads_target_elsewhere, foreach_reads_sibling_target) compare at
atol=rtol=1e-4; the other six stay on the default. The bug this test guards
(pytorch/pytorch#198549, a realized buffer swung in mutate_to) shows up as
~100% of elements wrong by order 100, so 1e-4 keeps four orders of magnitude
of detection margin.
Reproduction note. The CI job ran on an Intel Data Center GPU Max 1100
(PVC); this runner has Arc Pro B60 (BMG), where the compiled and eager results
are bitwise identical across seeds and all 8 cases pass unpatched. The
mismatch therefore cannot be reproduced here. Verification instead replayed the
CI deviation: injecting 1.52587890625e-05 onto an element of the reported
magnitude reproduces the CI assertion text verbatim and fails under the old
tolerance while passing under the new one.


Summary
The disabled test compares two 1024x1024 fp32 matmul results, one from
inductor's extern mm and one from eager, at assertEqual's default float32
tolerance, which is tighter than the rounding spread of a 1024-long reduction;
on the Max 1100 a single element of 1048576 fell outside it. The fix gives the
two mm-based cases of test_mutate_realized_buffer_in_make_fx_graph
atol=rtol=1e-4 in pytorch, leaving the six pointwise cases exact. Verified
on a source build at the CI commit: the family passes on CPU and XPU (16
passed), and the exact CI deviation, replayed on an element of the reported
magnitude, fails the old tolerance and passes the new one.

Root Cause
Analyzed at pytorch origin/main@393b3877.
test_update_weights builds an nn.Linear(4096, 2048) and compares an eager invocation against the AOTInductor-compiled one at test/inductor/test_aot_inductor_package.py:1237-1239, using assertEqual's fp32 defaults (atol=1e-5, rtol=1.3e-6). Both sides bottom out in the same XPU operator: eager nn.Linear lowers to at::addmm(bias, input, weight.t()), and the generated AOTI wrapper emits aoti_torch_xpu_addmm_out(buf0, linear_bias, arg2_1, reinterpret_tensor(linear_weight, ...)) (confirmed by dumping TORCH_LOGS=output_code for the test's model). So the test is not comparing two different algorithms -- it is comparing two invocations of one GEMM.
The reason that comparison can fail is that the XPU fp32 GEMM is not run-to-run deterministic at this shape. Calling torch.nn.functional.linear twice on identical inputs (M, N, K = 128, 2048, 4096) differs on this machine in 50 out of 50 repeats, with a greatest absolute difference of 3.0518e-05; the same holds for the bare x @ w.t() with no bias. Shrinking the reduction to K=512 or K=64 makes it bit-exact in 50/50 repeats, which is the signature of oneDNN selecting a split-K GEMM whose partial-sum reduction order varies between launches only once K is large enough. The spread is on the order of 1 ULP of the accumulator scale (outputs here have magnitude up to ~330, ulp(330) = 3.05e-05), and it is an absolute perturbation, independent of how large the output element itself is.
That is what makes atol=1e-5 unsound for this test. For an output element that lands near zero -- plentiful among the 262144 outputs, since they are sums of 4096 products that cancel -- the rtol term contributes essentially nothing, so the whole budget is 1e-5, below the perturbation the non-deterministic reduction can inject. The upstream CI failure is exactly that element: Greatest absolute difference: 1.1444091796875e-05 at index (29, 500) (up to 1e-05 allowed) against an output value of ~0.207. The margin is device-dependent, which is why this is a PVC-only failure in practice: measured as a fraction of the assertEqual budget, the worst case over 150+ randomized draws on BMG is 0.38x, whereas the PVC log shows 1.14x.
Fix strategy: widen the tolerance for this one test rather than chase GEMM bit-reproducibility. The test exercises load_constants, not matmul numerics -- a weight that failed to update would be wrong by O(1), some four orders of magnitude above any tolerance discussed here -- so atol=1e-4 (about 9x the worst observed PVC perturbation, about 3x the worst absolute difference measured anywhere) keeps the assertion meaningful while putting it safely above ULP-level noise. Both comparisons in the test need it: the self.check_model(...) call at line 1226 compares eager against compiled over the same K=4096 GEMM and has identical exposure, it simply happened to land under the threshold in the failing CI run. The surrounding tests in this file all use 10x10 shapes, so scoping the change to test_update_weights leaves every other tolerance in the file untouched. Making the GEMM itself reproducible would be a oneDNN-level change and is out of scope here.

Field

Verdict
IMPLEMENTING



Not a flex-decoding bug. Measured against an fp64 CPU reference, the compiled
flex-decoding kernel is exact (3e-07) and the eager reference the test compares
against is the inaccurate side (1.3e-03). The compiled kernel is generated with
FLOAT32_PRECISION='ieee', so the 1e-3 gap is TF32 in the eager XPU matmuls.
XPU eager matmul precision is gated by one switch that nothing else writes:
at::globalContext().allowTF32OneDNN() (exposed as torch.backends.mkldnn.allow_tf32,
read in aten/src/ATen/native/mkldnn/xpu/detail/Matmul.cpp). It is not touched by
torch.set_float32_matmul_precision() or by the fp32_precision / allow_tf32
setters for the cuda and mkldnn backends.
test/inductor/test_flex_decoding.py turns that switch on at import time
(torch._C._set_onednn_allow_tf32(True) when running on XPU), mirroring the
module's set_float32_matmul_precision("high") so the loose-tolerance tests
exercise the same reduced-precision paths CUDA does.
test_pointwise_query_producer (added by pytorch/pytorch#198543, compares with
assertEqual's default fp32 tolerances rtol=1.3e-6, atol=1e-5) is decorated
@with_tf32_off. On CUDA that decorator delivers full fp32 on both sides. On XPU it
sets the cuda/mkldnn fp32_precision values to ieee but leaves the oneDNN TF32
switch on, so the eager reference keeps running in TF32 and the comparison fails by
~1.3e-3. Confirmed in-test: cuda.matmul=ieee, mkldnn.matmul=tf32,
onednn_allow_tf32=True, and a bare q @ k.transpose(-2, -1) in that same context
is off by 1.0e-02.
So the gap is in test infrastructure: tf32_off() in
torch/testing/_internal/common_cuda.py does not cover the XPU oneDNN TF32 flag,
even though with_tf32_off's contract is "enforce torch.float tensors to be always
computed at full precision". test/inductor/test_flex_attention.py already works
around this by hand in its local temp_float32_matmul_precision helper.
Fix strategy: make tf32_off() also clear the oneDNN TF32 switch on XPU builds,
and save/restore it alongside the other matmul-precision state so the context manager
stays leak-free. The alternative -- having
torch.set_float32_matmul_precision() / setAllowTF32CuBLAS drive
allow_tf32_onednn in aten/src/ATen/Context.cpp -- would change user-visible eager
precision across all of XPU and is far beyond what this disabled test needs.
Automated by fix-root-cause.



Implement Result
diff --git a/torch/testing/_internal/common_cuda.py b/torch/testing/_internal/common_cuda.py
--- a/torch/testing/_internal/common_cuda.py
+++ b/torch/testing/_internal/common_cuda.py
@@ -469,11 +469,12 @@ _tf32_off_cudnn_ctx = None
 def _save_matmul_precision():
     return (_get_legacy_float32_matmul_precision(),
             torch.backends.cuda.matmul.fp32_precision,
-            torch.backends.mkldnn.matmul.fp32_precision)
+            torch.backends.mkldnn.matmul.fp32_precision,
+            torch._C._get_onednn_allow_tf32() if torch.xpu.is_available() else None)
 
 
 def _restore_matmul_precision(saved):
-    legacy, cuda_precision, mkldnn_precision = saved
+    legacy, cuda_precision, mkldnn_precision, onednn_allow_tf32 = saved
     # set_float32_matmul_precision overwrites both backend-specific values, so
     # it goes first. Restoring those as fp32_precision strings rather than as
     # allow_tf32 booleans also preserves the "none" default, which allow_tf32
@@ -481,6 +482,8 @@ def _restore_matmul_precision(saved):
     _set_legacy_float32_matmul_precision(legacy)
     torch.backends.cuda.matmul.fp32_precision = cuda_precision
     torch.backends.mkldnn.matmul.fp32_precision = mkldnn_precision
+    if onednn_allow_tf32 is not None:
+        torch._C._set_onednn_allow_tf32(onednn_allow_tf32)
 
 
 @contextlib.contextmanager
@@ -495,6 +498,10 @@ def tf32_off():
         if _tf32_off_depth == 0:
             _tf32_off_saved_precision = _save_matmul_precision()
             torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = False
+            # XPU eager matmul reads a separate oneDNN TF32 switch that none of
+            # the fp32_precision / allow_tf32 setters above write.
+            if torch.xpu.is_available():
+                torch._C._set_onednn_allow_tf32(False)
             _tf32_off_cudnn_ctx = torch.backends.cudnn.flags(enabled=None, benchmark=None, deterministic=None, allow_tf32=False)
             _tf32_off_cudnn_ctx.__enter__()
         _tf32_off_depth += 1
The torch._C._set_onednn_allow_tf32 setter warns on builds without XPU support, so
both the save and the clear are guarded by torch.xpu.is_available(); non-XPU
platforms are byte-for-byte unaffected. tf32_on() is deliberately left alone --
making it enable the switch would change what tf32_on_and_off tests measure on XPU.

test/inductor/test_torchinductor_dynamic_shapes.py::DynamicShapesGPUTests::test_mutate_realized_buffer_in_make_fx_graph_case_foreach_reads_sibling_target_dynamic_shapes_xpu
fails with Tensor-likes are not close!, 1 mismatched element out of
1048576, greatest absolute difference 1.5e-05 against atol=1e-05. The
failure is flaky run to run, not seed dependent, which is why it only shows
up on some shards.
Root cause. The case computes a = x @ w1 and b = x @ w2 on
1024x1024 float32 and compares the inductor result against an independently
computed eager result at the default float32 tolerance. Both runs add the
two mms together, which cancels and leaves elements near zero, so the
comparison rests entirely on atol=1e-05 — rtol buys nothing at those
magnitudes. The XPU float32 GEMM is not run-to-run bit-exact at this size:
two back-to-back eager x @ w calls already differ by up to 1.5e-05,
which is the whole atol budget. Both results are equally accurate against a
float64 reference (1.46e-04 each), so neither side is wrong, and the
mutation ordering the test actually checks is never involved. x @ w
becomes bit-stable again under torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True),
consistent with a GEMM that splits the reduction dimension by default.
Fix. Draw that one case's inputs from small integers instead of randn,
so the 1024-term dot products are exactly representable in float32 and any
GEMM reproduces them bit-for-bit whatever order it accumulates in. The
assertion keeps its tight tolerance. This is the idiom
test_index_put_as_masked_fill_mask_reads_target_by_extern_kernel and
test_mutable_op_layout_copy_written_back_in_place already use in the same
file. Loosening the tolerance instead would also have worked, but exactness
costs nothing here: a wrong mutation order changes elements by order of
their own magnitude, not by 1e-05.
The other mm-bearing case, foreach_reads_target_elsewhere, is left alone:
its single x @ x.t() keeps elements large enough for rtol to cover the
same GEMM spread, and it passed 8 of 8 runs unmodified.
Verification. 20/20 passes of the previously failing test, plus the full
parametrized family green on cpu and xpu across all three generated suites
(16 + 16 + 24 tests). ruff 0.14.4 format and check are clean on the
changed file.


Summary
The disabled test compared two independently computed 1024x1024 float32
matmuls at the default float32 tolerance, and because the two mms cancel,
the surviving budget was atol=1e-05 while the XPU GEMM's own run-to-run
spread is 1.5e-05 — so it failed about 60% of the time regardless of seed.
The fix makes that case's inputs integral, which makes the mms exact and the
comparison backend-independent without relaxing the tolerance that guards
the mutation ordering under test. After the change the test passed 20 of 20
runs and the whole parametrized family passed on cpu and xpu in all three
generated suites.

issues.title: FA4 backend is not supported on XPU
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

test/nn/attention/test_fa4.py currently only instantiates CUDA device tests. We want to enable XPU test collection for this file so that the coverage matrix reflects XPU. However, FA4 itself is currently CUDA-specific and is not supported by the XPU backend.

The FA4 tests depend on CUDA-only capability checks and the `flash_attn.cute.interface` package:

```
def _fa4_dependencies_available() -> bool:
    if not torch.cuda.is_available():
        return False
    major, _ = torch.cuda.get_device_capability(torch.cuda.current_device())
    if major not in (9, 10):
        return False

importlib.import_module("flash_attn.cute.interface")

```




### Versions

Pytorch 2.14

issues.title: [profiler] XPU kernel activities lack stream/grid/block metadata expected by upstream Kineto trace tests
issues.body:
## Summary

XPU kernel activities in a Kineto chrome trace do not carry the `stream`, `grid` and `block` metadata keys that CUDA and ROCm emit. `device` and `correlation` are fine. This makes `test/profiler/test_profiler.py::TestProfilerDevice::test_kineto_kernel_metadata_in_trace` fail on XPU. It is a latent gap, not a regression: the class is instantiated without `allow_xpu=True`, so the test had never run on XPU until we enabled it.

| Key asserted by the test | CUDA | ROCm | XPU |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `device`, `correlation` | yes | yes | yes |
| `stream` | yes | yes | no (`sycl queue` / `l0 queue` instead) |
| `grid`, `block` | yes | yes | no |

```
AssertionError: 'stream' not found in {..., 'correlation': 1023, 'device': 0, 'l0 queue': '0x...', 'sycl queue': 64}
kernel 'gemm_kernel' missing 'stream'
```

`stream` fails first, but `grid`/`block` are a second independent gap: the trailing `has_kernel_launch_metadata` assertion would fail too.

## Where

- `libkineto/src/plugin/xpupti/XpuptiActivityHandlers.cpp`, `XpuptiActivityProfilerSession::handleRuntimeKernelMemcpyMemsetActivities()` never emits the three keys. `libkineto/include/MetadataFieldCatalog.h` confirms it: `XpuMetadataFields` has no `kStream`, `kGrid` or `kBlock`, while `CudaMetadataFields` and `RocmMetadataFields` define all three.
- Costs differ a lot between the two halves. `stream` is nearly free: `_sycl_queue_id` is already collected and emitted, just named `sycl queue`. `grid`/`block` look blocked in PTI 1.1.0 (oneAPI 2026.1): neither `pti_view_record_kernel` nor `_v2` in `pti/pti_view.h` carries any work-group count or size.

## Repro

Add `allow_xpu=True` to the `instantiate_device_type_tests(TestProfilerDevice, globals())` call in `test/profiler/test_profiler.py`, then:

```
python -m pytest test/profiler/test_profiler.py -k test_kineto_kernel_metadata_in_trace_xpu -v
```

Or without the harness:

```python
import json, torch
from torch.profiler import profile, ProfilerActivity

x = torch.randn(128, 128, device="xpu")
with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.XPU]) as prof:
    torch.mm(x, x)
    torch.xpu.synchronize()
prof.export_chrome_trace("t.json")
for e in json.load(open("t.json"))["traceEvents"]:
    if e.get("cat") == "kernel":
        print(e["name"], sorted(e.get("args", {})))
```

## Impact

About 5 upstream test IDs: this one, plus the 4 in `TestMetadataJsonFormat`, which asserts `common_keys = ["device", "stream", "correlation", "grid", "block"]` for every backend and so can never be enabled on XPU as written. We are skipping the failing test on XPU pointing at this issue so the rest of the newly enabled `TestProfilerDevice` XPU coverage can land.

## Question

Should xpupti emit `stream` (and eventually `grid`/`block`), or should an XPU-specific key set be agreed and the upstream test branch on backend the way it already does for ROCm (`expected = common_keys if TEST_WITH_ROCM else common_keys + cuda_only_keys`)? Given `grid`/`block` appear unavailable from PTI, is exposing work-group count and size in the kernel view records planned?

## Environment

PyTorch `2.15.0a0+gita56a3a1`, `torch.version.xpu = 20260101`, kineto `8b682ab`, Intel Data Center GPU Max 1550 (driver `1.6.33578+77`), oneAPI 2026.1.1 / PTI 1.1.0, kernel `6.17.0-35-generic`.

issues.title: test_masked_scatter_xpu_complex128 and  test_masked_scatter_xpu_complex64 failed
issues.body:
## Description
`test/test_torch.py::TestTorchDeviceTypeXPU::test_masked_scatter_xpu_complex128` aborts the entire Python process instead of failing/passing cleanly.

The test intentionally calls `masked_scatter_` with an undersized `src` and, for non-CUDA devices, expects a catchable `RuntimeError`:

```python
if self.device_type != 'cuda':
    # make src smaller. this should fail
    src = torch.zeros(num_copy - 1, dtype=dt, device=device)
    with self.assertRaises(RuntimeError):
        dest.masked_scatter_(mask, src)
```

On XPU the bounds check is a device-side assert in `src/ATen/native/xpu/sycl/Indexing.cpp:446` (`Assertion totalElements <= srcSize_ failed`). It aborts the process (`Fatal Python error: Aborted`) rather than raising a Python-catchable `RuntimeError`, so `assertRaises(RuntimeError)` cannot catch it. This matches the CUDA behavior the test explicitly excludes.

## Error log
```
AssertHandler::printMessage
/__w/pytorch/pytorch/third_party/torch-xpu-ops/src/ATen/native/xpu/sycl/Indexing.cpp:446: operator(): global id: [0,0,0], local id: [0,0,0] Assertion `totalElements <= srcSize_` failed.
Fatal Python error: Aborted
```

## Reproduce
On a PVC machine, using pytorch/pytorch#196421:
```
python test/test_torch.py TestTorchDeviceTypeXPU.test_masked_scatter_xpu_complex128
```

## Expected
`masked_scatter_` with an undersized `src` on XPU should raise a recoverable `RuntimeError` (matching CPU), or XPU should be treated like CUDA and excluded from the recover-and-catch branch of this test.

## Environment
- PyTorch: `2.15.0.dev20260907+xpu`
- Device: Intel(R) Data Center GPU Max 1550 (PVC)
- Reproduced with pytorch/pytorch#196421

issues.title: [profiler] os.fork() deadlocks after Kineto XPU profiler initialization
issues.body:
## Summary

`os.fork()` deadlocks if the parent process has already initialized Kineto's XPU profiler. The child hangs before completing its own profiling session and the parent blocks forever in `os.waitpid()`. This breaks `test/profiler/test_profiler.py::TestProfilerDevice::test_forked_process` on any XPU build, and it is order-dependent today: the test passes in isolation (~2s) and only hangs once some earlier test in the same process has brought up the XPU profiler. That ordering is not guaranteed under test sharding.

## Repro

Deadlocks (killed by `timeout`, never prints "reaped"):

```python
import os, torch
from torch.profiler import profile, ProfilerActivity

# Initialize Kineto's XPU profiler in the parent.
x = torch.ones(1, device="xpu")
with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.XPU]):
    x + x
    torch.xpu.synchronize()

pid = os.fork()
if pid == 0:
    with profile(activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU]):
        torch.ones(1) + torch.ones(1)
    os._exit(0)
print("parent: waiting on child", pid, flush=True)
print("parent: reaped", os.waitpid(pid, 0), flush=True)
```

Control: drop the XPU-primed block and make the parent's first session CPU-only, and the same fork reaps cleanly (`parent: reaped (192423, 0)`). So the trigger is specifically XPU profiler initialization in the parent, not fork-plus-profiler in general.

Stacks when hung: the child sits in `futex_do_wait`, the parent in `do_wait` under `os.waitpid`. Note the parent never observes the child's assertions, so a dead child would still report PASS if the wait ever returned.

## Impact

- `test_forked_process` cannot run on XPU builds. We are skipping it at process level (gated on the build, not on `device_type`, because the test is `@onlyOn("cpu")` so a device-scoped skip would never fire) while enabling XPU on the rest of `TestProfilerDevice` upstream.
- This costs the CPU coverage of that test on XPU machines specifically; CPU-only and CUDA builds keep it.
- The torch-xpu-ops test fork already works around it: `test/xpu/profiler/test_profiler_xpu.py` carries `@unittest.skipIf(torch.xpu.is_available(), "XPU complains about forking after init")`.

## Possibly related

- #2261 (closed) covers PTI `sycl_collector` *warnings* after fork ("Another subscriber already subscribed to Sycl runtime events"), not a deadlock.
- #2089 (closed) on `torch.xpu.is_available()` initializing a GPU context is adjacent root-cause context.

## Environment

PyTorch `2.15.0a0+gita56a3a1`, `torch.version.xpu = 20260101`, kineto `8b682ab`, Intel Data Center GPU Max 1550 (driver `1.6.33578+77`), oneAPI 2026.1.1 / PTI 1.1.0, kernel `6.17.0-35-generic`.

issues.title: [upstream_ut] test_torch.py nondeterministic_alert failures: XPU backward kernels raise stale non-deterministic error
issues.body:
## Description
25 `test_nondeterministic_alert_*` cases in `test/test_torch.py` fail on XPU. The tests do NOT expect a non-determinism error in the default (non-deterministic) mode, but the XPU backward kernels still raise:

    RuntimeError: <op>_backward_xpu does not have a deterministic implementation, but you set 'torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)'...

producing: "did not expect non-deterministic error message, but got one anyway".

This resembles previously fixed issues (#3117 stale alertNotDeterministic on scatter kernels, #2512/#2516/#2517) and looks like a stale/over-broad `alertNotDeterministic` on additional ops.

## Affected tests

Match CUDA behavior: these ops should not raise a non-determinism error in the default mode (they should either be deterministic or not flagged when use_deterministic_algorithms is False).

issues.title: [skip-added] test_effn_attn_uniform_zero_bias on XPU: SDPA never selects the efficient-attention backend
issues.body:
Auto-added by `fix-implement` (allow_skip=true), from the batch fan-out on intel/torch-xpu-ops#5272.

**Test:** `test/inductor/test_cuda_repro.py::CudaReproTests::test_effn_attn_uniform_zero_bias`
(upstream DISABLED test: pytorch/pytorch#196552)

**Original failure:** `AssertionError: 0 != 1` at `test_cuda_repro.py:298` (`self.assertEqual(len(biases), 1)`),
reached from `test_cuda_repro.py:328` -- the phase that traces
`F.scaled_dot_product_attention(..., attn_mask=padding_mask)` under
`sdpa_kernel(SDPBackend.EFFICIENT_ATTENTION)` and expects exactly one
`aten._scaled_dot_product_efficient_attention` node in the joint graph.

**Root cause:** `select_sdp_backend_xpu` returns the *math* backend from its
`efficient_attention` case (`aten/src/ATen/native/mkldnn/xpu/Attention.cpp:224-231`):

```cpp
      case sdp::SDPBackend::efficient_attention:
        if (ctx.userEnabledMemEfficientSDP() &&
            can_use_mem_efficient_attention(kernel_params, print_debug)) {
          TORCH_WARN_ONCE(
              "SDPA Memory Efficient Attention backend is not supported on XPU, falling back to math backend.");
          return sdp::SDPBackend::math;
        }
```

So on XPU, `F.scaled_dot_product_attention` under
`sdpa_kernel(SDPBackend.EFFICIENT_ATTENTION)` traces to the math decomposition and
never emits an `_scaled_dot_product_efficient_attention` call for the test's
`joint_custom_post_pass` to capture. The earlier phases of the same test pass
because they invoke `aten._scaled_dot_product_efficient_attention.default`
directly, bypassing backend selection.

**Reason for skip:** making the XPU SDPA dispatcher actually select
`efficient_attention` is a capability change, not a test fix: `_fused_sdp_choice_xpu`
would have to stop routing to math, and XPU's
`_scaled_dot_product_efficient_attention_backward` currently re-runs the whole math
forward under autograd, so flipping the selection would be a behavioral and
performance change well beyond this failure. That decision belongs to the XPU SDPA
owners.

**Base analyzed:** pytorch@31527a43

Follow-up: either implement/enable efficient-attention backend selection on XPU and
remove the `@skipIfXpu`, or confirm the math fallback is intentional and upstream a
permanent test-side exclusion.

issues.title: [XPU] Integer matmul tests fail due to unsupported int types in dot_xpu_mkl and oneDNN
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Several matmul tests that check integer type support (int16, int32, int64) are skipped on XPU due to backend limitations. The dot_xpu_mkl and oneDNN kernels currently dispatch only for floating-point and complex types.

**Affected Tests (4 total):**
- `test_matmul_small_brute_force_1d_Nd[int16]`
- `test_matmul_small_brute_force_2d_Nd[int16]`
- `test_matmul_small_brute_force_3d_Nd[int16]`
- `test_corner_cases_of_cublasltmatmul[int16]`

**Root Cause:**
The XPU dispatch path for matmul operations (via dot_xpu_mkl and oneDNN kernels) does not support integer types (int16, int32, int64). When these types are used, the operation falls back to CPU execution or fails entirely on XPU devices.

issues.title: [XPU] aten::_dyn_quant_pack_4bit_weight not implemented, causing dyn_quant tests to skip
issues.body:
Dynamic quantization tests that use 4-bit weight packing are skipped on XPU due to missing kernel implementation. The aten::_dyn_quant_pack_4bit_weight operator is not registered for the XPU device, causing all dependent tests to skip.

Affected Tests (3 total):

test__dyn_quant_pack_4bit_weight[xpu]
test__dyn_quant_matmul_4bit[xpu]
test_compile_dyn_quant_matmul_4bit[xpu]
Root Cause:
The aten::_dyn_quant_pack_4bit_weight operator used for dynamic quantization in PyTorch does not have a kernel implementation for XPU devices. This is a PyTorch quantization utility operator, not a standard matrix operation.

issues.title: [inductor][distributed] Inductor cudagraphs silently no-op on XPU: cudagraph_trees needs XPU allocator checkpoint bindings (`_xpu_getCheckpointState` et al.)
issues.body:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.compile` with `torch._inductor.config.triton.cudagraphs = True` silently does
nothing on XPU. The flag *is* read and inductor reaches its device check, which only
clears CUDA, so cudagraphs are skipped — and a test that asserts "graphs work" passes
without ever capturing one.

```bash
python - <<'EOF'
import torch
with torch._inductor.config.patch({"triton.cudagraphs": True}):
    f = torch.compile(lambda x: (x + 1).sum(), backend="inductor", fullgraph=True)
    inp = torch.randn(2, 8, device="xpu:1")
    for _ in range(3):
        out = f(inp)
print("out:", out.device)
EOF
```

```
W torch/_inductor/cudagraph_utils.py:401] [__cudagraphs] skipping cudagraphs due to skipping cudagraphs due to multiple devices: device(type='xpu', index=1)
out: xpu:1
```

The "multiple devices" wording is misleading — there is a single XPU device; the check
simply does not accept a non-CUDA device.

There are two blockers, in order:

**1. The gate.** `torch/_inductor/cudagraph_utils.py`,
`check_multiple_devices_or_any_cpu_nodes()` only clears a device whose `.type == "cuda"`:

```python
if (
    len(device_node_mapping) == 1
    and next(iter(device_node_mapping.keys())).type == "cuda"
):
    return None
```

**2. The runtime.** With that check relaxed to accept `xpu`, capture then dies:

```
File "torch/_inductor/cudagraph_trees.py", line 2377, in __init__
    with graph_capture_lock, torch.cuda.device(device_index):
File "torch/cuda/__init__.py", line 181, in _exchange_device
    raise RuntimeError("PyTorch was compiled without CUDA support")
```

`cudagraph_trees.py` has 64 CUDA call sites across 22 distinct APIs. Most already map
1:1 onto `torch.xpu` — `synchronize`, `device`, `current_stream`, `Stream`, `stream`,
`graph`, `graph_pool_handle`, `current_device`, `memory`, `memory_snapshot`,
`is_initialized` are all present, plus `XPUGraph` where CUDA has `CUDAGraph` — and the
three core pool hooks exist as `torch._C._xpu_beginAllocateCurrentThreadToPool`,
`_xpu_endAllocateToPool`, `_xpu_releasePool`.

What is missing on the XPU side:

| CUDA binding | XPU equivalent | Used at | Needed for |
|---|---|---|---|
| `_cuda_getCheckpointState` | **missing** | `cudagraph_trees.py:1612`, in `_add_first_outputs` | **first recording of every graph** |
| `_cuda_setCheckpointPoolState` | **missing** | `:3257` | restoring allocator state when re-entering a recorded graph |
| `_cuda_cudaCachingAllocator_raw_delete` | **missing** | `:3267` | freeing outputs during that restore |
| `_cuda_checkPoolLiveAllocations` | **missing** | `:2215` | live-allocation asserts |
| `_cuda_isHistoryEnabled` | **missing** (XPU has `_xpu_recordMemoryHistory`) | `:203` | memory-history debug |

Because `_cuda_getCheckpointState` sits on the *first recording* path, this cannot be
worked around in Python: XPU cannot capture even a single graph through
`cudagraph_trees` today.

### Suggested fix

1. **XPU allocator (this repo):** add the missing bindings above — at minimum
   `_xpu_getCheckpointState`, `_xpu_setCheckpointPoolState` and an XPU `raw_delete`,
   since those three gate capture and replay.
2. **PyTorch inductor (separate PR):** make `cudagraph_utils` accept the current
   accelerator and route `cudagraph_trees` through
   `torch.get_device_module(device_type)`, aliasing `CUDAGraph`/`XPUGraph`. A
   `torch._inductor.config.triton.xpugraphs` switch would let tests select the XPU path
   explicitly while `triton.cudagraphs` remains the CUDA one. No such option exists
   today — `hasattr(config.triton, "xpugraphs")` is `False`, and patching it raises
   `AttributeError: torch._inductor.config.triton.xpugraphs does not exist`.

### Test impact

While porting `test/distributed/tensor/test_compile_on_one_rank.py` to be
device-agnostic (pytorch/pytorch#114850), 29 of its 30 tests were enabled on XPU. The
one exception is
`TestCompileOnOneRankDeviceAsParameter::test_cudagraphs_under_coor_runs_on_nonzero_device`,
which had to be marked `@skipIfXpu(msg="inductor cudagraphs is CUDA-only")`: with the
skip removed it *passes in 2.7s without recording a graph* — green but vacuous, which
is worse than an explicit skip.

Note that `torch.xpu.XPUGraph`, `torch.xpu.graph` and `torch.xpu.make_graphed_callables`
all work in eager mode. The gap is only that inductor never routes to them.

Related: #3570 skips the xccl collective graph-replay UTs (`test_allreduce_graph_replay`
et al.), which is c10d-level graph capture; this issue is about inductor's graph path.

### Versions

```
torch              2.15.0a0+git28789c4  (source build, commit 28789c4f989)
torch.version.xpu  20260100
triton-xpu         3.8.0+git1e2d42a0
device             4x Intel(R) Data Center GPU Max 1100
backend            xccl
```

issues.title: [xpu-alignment] [26-09-13] torch.add(dense, dense, out=sparse_csr) aborts the process on XPU instead of raising
issues.body:
<!-- alignment-published-unit: issue-196906 -->
## Summary

On XPU, `torch.add(a, b, out=out)` with strided `a` and `b` and a valid sparse CSR `out` terminates the process with SIGSEGV and no Python-level exception. Upstream CPU raises a catchable (if unpolished) `RuntimeError: ... INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED`, so an XPU user gets strictly less than upstream: no diagnosable error at all, and no chance to handle it.

The layout combination itself need not be supported. The defect is that `add_out_sparse_compressed_xpu` re-dispatches instead of rejecting it, so the call never terminates.

## Upstream source

- pytorch/pytorch#196906, "torch.add with dense inputs and valid sparse CSR out triggers INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED", created 2026-09-13T15:45:32Z, reported on CPU/CUDA build 2.13.0+cu126. Still OPEN with no linked fix PR or cross-referenced commit as of 2026-09-14.
- Found by an xpu-alignment scan of the half-open window `[2026-09-13T00:00:00Z, 2026-09-14T00:00:00Z)` against the `pytorch/pytorch` default-branch snapshot `ad9448bc18658ff31d7512c2e5368f0718cf1ea0`.

## Observed XPU behavior

Runner result: `returncode -11` (SIGSEGV), `timed_out: false`, 8.049 s, no `RESULT` token, no traceback.

```text
torch_version: 2.15.0.dev20260912+xpu
xpu_available: True
xpu_device_name: Intel(R) Arc(TM) Pro B60 Graphics
control_layout: torch.sparse_csr
control_device: xpu:0
control_dense: [[3.0, 0.0], [0.0, 3.0]]
a_layout_device: torch.strided xpu:0
b_layout_device: torch.strided xpu:0
out_layout_device: torch.sparse_csr xpu:0
marker: calling torch.add(dense, dense, out=sparse_csr)
```

## Target-path evidence

- `aten/src/ATen/native/native_functions.yaml` at the snapshot dispatches `add.out` for `SparseCsrXPU` to `add_out_sparse_compressed_xpu`, which this repository implements.
- The control call (sparse CSR + sparse CSR) ran first and returned `torch.sparse_csr` on `xpu:0` densifying to `[[3.0, 0.0], [0.0, 3.0]]`, so the `SparseCsrXPU` add path is reachable and functional on this device. No XPU-to-CPU fallback warning was emitted for `add` (the one fallback warning in the log comes from sparse CSR construction).
- The operand layouts and devices were printed immediately before the call, and the reproducer runs under `python -u`, so the pre-call marker being the last line places the abort inside the target call, not in setup and not after it.

## Root cause

`src/ATen/native/sparse/xpu/SparseCsrTensorMath.cpp:400`:

```cpp
Tensor& add_out_sparse_compressed_xpu(
    const Tensor& self,
    const SparseCsrTensor& other,
    const Scalar& alpha,
    SparseCsrTensor& out) {
  if (self.layout() == kStrided) {
    at::add_out(out, self, other.to_dense(), alpha);
    return out;
  } else if (other.layout() == kStrided) {
    at::add_out(out, other, self.to_dense(), alpha);
    return out;
  }
```

`Tensor::to_dense()` on a strided tensor returns that tensor unchanged, so when both inputs are strided and `out` is sparse CSR the re-dispatch of `at::add_out` selects `SparseCsrXPU` again (the key comes from `out`) with identical layouts. That recurses without bound and exhausts the native stack, which Python cannot convert into `RecursionError`; the reproducer catches `RecursionError` explicitly and it never fired.

The log contains no native backtrace, so the recursion mechanism is inferred from the source above; what the run directly establishes is an uncatchable process abort inside the target call.

The second branch has the same trap: `add(sparse_csr, dense, out=sparse_csr)` enters `else if (other.layout() == kStrided)`, re-dispatches with two strided inputs, and then takes the first branch. Both branches need the guard.

Suggested fix: `TORCH_CHECK` the supported `out` layout (strided when either input is strided) before re-dispatching, so the unsupported combination produces a user-facing error instead of unbounded re-entry.

## Ownership

Upstream CPU takes a different branch for the same inputs: `add_out_sparse_compressed_cpu` calls `add_out_dense_sparse_compressed_cpu(out, self, other, alpha)`, whose `TORCH_INTERNAL_ASSERT(src.layout() == kSparseCsr || src.layout() == kSparseCsc)` is the assertion pytorch/pytorch#196906 reports. Fixing that CPU entry point, or improving its error message, does not touch `add_out_sparse_compressed_xpu`, which is separate code in this repository. No `pytorch/pytorch` issue or PR owns the XPU function, and a search of `intel/torch-xpu-ops` (sparse csr add, add_out_sparse_compressed, SparseCsrTensorMath, xpu-alignment) found no existing tracker.

## Reproducer

```python
import torch

def make_csr(values):
    return torch.sparse_csr_tensor(
        torch.tensor([0, 1, 2], device="xpu"),
        torch.tensor([0, 1], device="xpu"),
        values,
        size=(2, 2),
        check_invariants=True,
        device="xpu",
    )

# Control: the SparseCsrXPU add path works.
control = torch.add(
    make_csr(torch.ones(2, device="xpu")),
    make_csr(torch.full((2,), 2.0, device="xpu")),
)
print(control.to_dense().cpu().tolist())

a = torch.ones((2, 2), device="xpu")
b = torch.ones((2, 2), device="xpu")
out = make_csr(torch.zeros(2, device="xpu"))
print("calling torch.add(dense, dense, out=sparse_csr)", flush=True)
torch.add(a, b, out=out)  # SIGSEGV on XPU; RuntimeError (INTERNAL ASSERT) on CPU
```

## Environment

- `torch 2.15.0.dev20260912+xpu` at `/opt/conda/lib/python3.13/site-packages/torch/__init__.py`
- Python 3.13.13 (`/opt/conda/bin/python3.13`), run as `python3.13 -I -u`
- `xpu_available: true`, device `Intel(R) Arc(TM) Pro B60 Graphics`, no environment warnings
- Run artifacts: `scripts/repro_issue-196906.py` (sha256 `b730db66dd4aba7eec8b593baedbffb1b8935563f11b140dbd43dcd3b80b57b9`), `runner/logs/issue-196906.log` (sha256 `2460b822d987aa98c2387221e0a28da94a33c1de72376f16758e355217f27528`)
